---
title: "Colorado Net Migration by Age"
subtitle: "1990 to 2025"
---

```{r}
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)

# Statewide, sexes combined, five-year groups: the figures quoted below.
state <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("output", "netmig-comparison.csv"),
  col_types = readr::cols(countyfips = "c", caveat = "c")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000", sex_label == "Total", grouping == "five")

rate <- function(p, g) {
  state |>
    dplyr::filter(period == p, age_group == g) |>
    dplyr::pull(rate_per_1000)
}

annual <- function(p) {
  state |>
    dplyr::filter(period == p) |>
    dplyr::summarise(x = sum(netmig_annual)) |>
    dplyr::pull(x) |>
    scales::comma(accuracy = 100)
}

weakest_1990s <- state |>
  dplyr::filter(period == "1990-2000") |>
  dplyr::pull(rate_per_1000) |>
  min()
```

The State Demography Office and the Census Bureau publish county population by
age and total net migration by county, but not net migration *by age* below the
state level. This site estimates it as a demographic residual: for a group of
people followed through time, net migration is what is left once births and
deaths are removed from their population change.

$$
\text{NM} = \text{Pop}_{\text{end}} - \text{Pop}_{\text{start}} - \text{Births} + \text{Deaths}
$$

Four periods are covered — **1990–2000, 2000–2010, 2010–2020 and 2020–2025** —
plus any span inside 2020–2025, for Colorado and each of its 64 counties. Age
groups are **age at the end of the period**, so a group labelled 25–29 in
2010–2020 is the people who were 25–29 in 2020 and 15–19 in 2010. Everything is
built from public data; county deaths by age, which are confidential, are
estimated (see the report).

## The headline

Colorado's net migration has swung widely — about `r annual("1990-2000")` a
year in the 1990s, `r annual("2000-2010")` in the 2000s, `r annual("2010-2020")`
in the 2010s, and `r annual("2020-2025")` since 2020. But the *shape* of who came
has changed far more than the total.

```{r}
#| echo: false

shown <- c("5-9", "10-14", "20-24", "25-29", "30-34", "40-44", "50-54", "60-64", "70-74")

state |>
  dplyr::filter(age_group %in% shown) |>
  dplyr::select(period, `Age at end of period` = age_group, age_order, rate_per_1000) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = rate_per_1000) |>
  dplyr::arrange(age_order) |>
  dplyr::select(-age_order) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = -`Age at end of period`, decimals = 1) |>
  gt::tab_header(title = "Annual net migration per 1,000 people") |>
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = `Age at end of period` == "25-29")
  )
```

In the 1990s Colorado gained people at **every single age**, from infants to the
very old — the weakest group still ran at `r round(weakest_1990s, 1)` per 1,000 a
year. Nothing since has looked like that.

Today the peak is almost back to its 1990s height: 25–29 runs at
`r round(rate("2020-2025", "25-29"), 1)` per 1,000 a year against
`r round(rate("1990-2000", "25-29"), 1)` in the boom. But the base beneath it has
fallen away. Every group from 45–49 to 80–84 is now **negative**, and the flow
of school-age children has all but stopped.

So the state is not drawing fewer young adults than it used to. It is drawing
almost as many, and far fewer of everyone else.

## Caveat

The SDO county age estimates are themselves cohort-component output, built from
vital records plus administrative migration signals.
This recovers the net migration by age *implied by* those published estimates. It
is the right number for anyone working from them, but it inherits their
assumptions rather than testing them.
